summary:
Orbital Twin is a personalized astronaut health self-assessment tool designed for long-duration space missions. It learns each astronaut's individual health baseline, tracks daily measurements, and translates changes into an interactive, color-coded body map and trend charts.

The platform monitors nine health indicators across seven body systems, helping astronauts identify unusual patterns before they become serious. Unlike generic health thresholds, its scoring system compares readings against personal baselines and uses cumulative-sum drift detection to identify gradual changes over time.

Orbital Twin accounts for NASA's five major spaceflight hazards: radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile environments. Mission presets for the ISS, lunar base, Mars transit, and Mars surface adapt the monitoring experience to each environment.

Astronauts receive measurement instructions, plain-language explanations, AI-generated action plans, and supporting NASA/NIH research. Data can be entered manually or through an on-device MediaPipe camera measurement.

A key feature is delay-aware communication with Earth. Astronauts can send health reports through LoopMessage, while the platform adjusts its recommended actions based on communication delays. NASA DONKI integration also provides live solar energetic particle reports.
details: Orbital Twin — Project Details Orbital Twin is a personalized astronaut health self-assessment and monitoring platform designed for long-duration human space missions. As humans travel farther from Earth and prepare for missions to the Moon and Mars, access to immediate medical support becomes increasingly difficult. Communication delays, limited onboard resources, and the unique physical demands of spaceflight mean that astronauts need better ways to understand changes in their health and make informed decisions while waiting for guidance from Earth. Orbital Twin addresses this challenge by bringing personalized health monitoring, trend analysis, environmental awareness, and delay-aware communication into one interactive platform. How Orbital Twin Works At the center of Orbital Twin is the idea that every astronaut has a different physiological baseline. Traditional health-monitoring systems often rely on general population reference ranges or fixed thresholds. However, a measurement that is normal for one person may represent a significant change for another. Orbital Twin takes an individualized approach by learning what is typical for each astronaut and using that information to evaluate new measurements. The platform monitors nine health indicators across seven body systems. As measurements are collected over time, Orbital Twin builds an individual baseline and compares new readings against the astronaut's historical patterns. Its scoring system uses statistical methods, including median-based baseline calculations, measurements of normal variability, and cumulative-sum (CUSUM) drift detection. This allows the platform to identify both sudden deviations and gradual changes that may be difficult to recognize from individual readings alone. For example, an astronaut's resting heart rate may increase slightly each day without immediately crossing a conventional medical threshold. By examining the trend in relation to that astronaut's personal baseline, Orbital Twin can identify a sustained deviation and bring it to the astronaut's attention. The objective is to help recognize potentially concerning patterns earlier rather than waiting until a measurement reaches an extreme value. These results are presented through an interactive, color-coded body map and supporting trend charts. Astronauts can explore different body systems, review their measurements, understand which indicators have changed, and see explanations of why a particular trend may deserve attention. The platform also provides measurement instructions, plain-language explanations, AI-generated action plans, and supporting NASA and NIH research references. This helps make complex health information easier to interpret without requiring astronauts to understand the underlying statistical calculations. Mission-Specific Health Monitoring Astronaut health cannot be considered separately from the environment in which a mission takes place. The conditions aboard the International Space Station are different from those of a lunar base or a long-duration journey to Mars. Orbital Twin accounts for NASA's five major spaceflight hazards: radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile or closed environments. To accommodate these differences, the platform includes mission presets for the International Space Station, a lunar base, Mars transit, and the Martian surface. These presets allow the monitoring experience to be adapted to the selected mission environment and its associated challenges. This makes Orbital Twin more than a general health dashboard: it is designed around the changing conditions astronauts may encounter throughout different stages of human space exploration. Radiation is an especially important part of this approach. Exposure to space radiation can vary depending on mission location, solar activity, shielding, and time spent outside protected environments. Orbital Twin includes a radiation-monitoring experience that helps astronauts consider exposure alongside their other health measurements. Its NASA DONKI integration provides access to solar energetic particle event information, bringing space-weather context into the monitoring experience. By connecting environmental conditions with personal health information, the platform aims to give astronauts a more complete picture of the factors that may affect their well-being. Data Collection and On-Device Measurements Orbital Twin is designed to support multiple ways of collecting health information. Astronauts can enter measurements manually, allowing the platform to work with readings obtained through onboard instruments or other approved measurement processes. The platform also includes an on-device camera measurement feature using MediaPipe, providing another way to collect selected facial measurements. The purpose of supporting multiple input methods is to make daily monitoring practical and flexible. A health-monitoring platform for space missions should not assume that every measurement will always come from the same device or that an astronaut will have access to a particular external system. By supporting manual input and on-device measurement, Orbital Twin provides a flexible foundation for collecting and reviewing health information. Daily measurements feed into the astronaut's personal health history. As more information is collected, the platform can establish a more useful baseline, compare new readings against historical trends, and present changes in a format that is easy to review. The intention is to make health monitoring an ongoing part of the mission rather than an isolated activity performed only when an astronaut notices a problem. Delay-Aware Communication with Earth One of Orbital Twin's most important design considerations is the communication delay between astronauts and Earth. During a mission to Mars, communication delays can make immediate conversations with medical personnel impossible. Depending on the relative positions of Earth and Mars, a message may take many minutes to travel in either direction. This creates a situation in which astronauts may need to assess their condition and follow appropriate onboard procedures before receiving a response from Earth. Orbital Twin addresses this through its delay-aware communication workflow. Astronauts can prepare and send health reports through LoopMessage, allowing relevant health information and detected changes to be communicated to the flight team. The platform also considers the selected communication delay when presenting recommended actions and follow-up expectations. Instead of treating communication with Earth as an instantaneous exchange, Orbital Twin is designed around the reality that a report may be sent, remain unanswered for a period of time, and require the crew to continue following onboard procedures in the meantime. The goal is to keep Earth involved while giving astronauts the information they need to understand their health and take appropriate steps without making every decision dependent on an immediate response. User Interface and Design Process We placed significant emphasis on the user experience because a health-monitoring platform for astronauts must communicate important information clearly, consistently, and efficiently. The system may be used in stressful situations, during demanding mission schedules, or when astronauts have limited time to interpret a measurement. We therefore wanted the interface to make complex health information understandable without overwhelming the user. We used Figma during the design process to plan the interface, organize the different sections of the platform, and develop the visual direction before implementation. This helped us think through how astronauts would move between health indicators, body-system information, trend charts, radiation monitoring, daily check-ins, and communication tools. Prototyping the experience in Figma also allowed us to consider the overall information hierarchy and consistency across different screens. We additionally referenced Apple's Human Interface Guidelines (HIG) when making interface and usability decisions. Although Orbital Twin is not limited to Apple's ecosystem, these guidelines provided useful principles for designing an intuitive and accessible interface. We focused on clear visual hierarchy, consistent navigation, readable information, recognizable interface elements, meaningful use of color, and minimizing unnecessary complexity. The color-coded body map is an important part of this design approach. Rather than requiring astronauts to interpret multiple tables of numerical measurements before understanding their overall status, the body map provides a visual starting point. Astronauts can quickly identify areas that may require attention and then explore the underlying measurements and explanations. Trend charts provide additional context so that the user can understand how a measurement has changed over time rather than seeing only its latest value. We also considered the importance of presenting AI-generated explanations in plain language. A system that produces a complex score without explaining what it means would not be especially useful in a mission environment. Orbital Twin is designed to connect its monitoring results with understandable explanations, suggested actions, and supporting research so that users can better understand why a particular change was flagged. Technology and Tools Used Orbital Twin was developed using a combination of modern web technologies, backend services, data analysis methods, and interface-design tools. - React: Used to build the interactive user interface and organize the platform into reusable components. - TypeScript: Used for structured frontend development and improved reliability when working with application data and interface components. - Vite: Used as the frontend development and build environment. - Python: Used for backend development and health-data processing. - FastAPI: Used to create backend endpoints and connect the frontend with the application's health-monitoring functionality. - Supabase: Used for application data storage and persistence. - MediaPipe: Used for on-device camera-based measurement functionality. - Figma: Used to plan, prototype, and refine the user interface and overall user experience. - Apple Human Interface Guidelines: Referenced as a design framework for usability, navigation, visual hierarchy, consistency, and clarity. - NASA and NIH research resources: Used to inform the project's understanding of astronaut health, spaceflight hazards, and the importance of evidence-supported health information. - NASA DONKI: Used for solar-event information to bring space-weather context into the radiation-monitoring experience. - LoopMessage: Used as part of the platform's health-report communication workflow. The combination of these tools allowed us to develop a platform that brings together frontend interaction, backend processing, individualized health analysis, visual communication, and mission-related information in a single experience. Creativity and Innovation The most important creative aspect of Orbital Twin is the combination of personal health baselines with the unique environmental and communication challenges of space exploration. Rather than building another general health dashboard, we designed the platform around the specific circumstances of astronauts who may spend extended periods away from immediate medical support. Its individualized scoring system is a central part of this approach. By comparing measurements against an astronaut's own historical patterns and looking for sustained drift, Orbital Twin focuses on meaningful changes over time rather than treating every user as though they share the same normal values. Another important aspect is the connection between health monitoring and mission context. Radiation exposure, gravity conditions, isolation, and distance from Earth are not separate concerns during a space mission. They can influence the conditions in which astronauts live and work. Orbital Twin brings these considerations into the same platform so that astronauts can review their health information alongside relevant mission and environmental context. The delay-aware communication workflow also reflects a different way of thinking about medical support. On Earth, people often assume that they can contact a medical professional and receive a response relatively quickly. During deep-space missions, this assumption no longer holds. Orbital Twin is designed around a future in which astronauts need to understand their own health information, follow appropriate onboard procedures, and communicate with Earth asynchronously. Finally, the project emphasizes making technical health information understandable. Its interactive body map, trend charts, plain-language explanations, AI-generated action plans, and research references are intended to bridge the gap between collecting measurements and helping astronauts interpret them. Factors Considered and Intended Impact Throughout development, we considered several factors that are especially important for a health-monitoring system intended for human spaceflight: 1. Individual physiological differences: Every astronaut has a different normal range, so monitoring should account for personal baselines rather than relying exclusively on generic thresholds. 2. Gradual health changes: Some concerning patterns may develop over multiple days, making trend analysis and sustained-drift detection important. 3. Spaceflight hazards: Radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile environments create conditions that must be considered alongside health measurements. 4. Mission differences: The monitoring experience should account for the different environments of the ISS, lunar missions, Mars transit, and the Martian surface. 5. Communication delays: Astronauts may need to understand and respond to health concerns before receiving a response from Earth. 6. Ease of use: Health information must be presented clearly, with intuitive navigation, readable charts, and explanations that do not require specialized technical knowledge. 7. Data collection flexibility: Manual entry and on-device measurements provide multiple ways to collect information. 8. Research and evidence: Health explanations should be supported by relevant research and credible scientific resources. 9. Medical responsibility: A monitoring platform should support astronaut self-assessment and communication with medical teams rather than replace professional medical judgment or mission-approved procedures. The intended impact of Orbital Twin is to improve astronaut health awareness and support more informed decision-making during long-duration missions. By helping astronauts understand their personal health patterns, recognize unusual changes, consider relevant environmental conditions, and communicate findings with Earth, the platform aims to reduce the uncertainty associated with managing health far from home. As human space exploration moves toward longer missions and destinations such as the Moon and Mars, systems that support onboard health awareness will become increasingly important. Orbital Twin represents an approach to making personalized health monitoring more accessible, understandable, and adaptable to the realities of deep-space exploration. Ultimately, Orbital Twin is built around one central idea: astronauts should have the information they need to understand changes in their health, even when immediate support from Earth is unavailable.
